priors.statement: At matched configuration HSTU beats SASRec on every published dataset, so the attention block itself — not tuning — is where this repository's structural gain lives.
priors.evidence: README ML-1M: SASRec HR@10 0.2853 / NDCG@10 0.1603 against HSTU 0.3097 / 0.1720 (+8.6%). ML-20M: 0.2889 / 0.1621 against 0.3273 / 0.1895 (+13.3%). Amazon Books: 0.0306 / 0.0164 against 0.0416 / 0.0227 (+36.4%). The README states the HSTU rows use identical configurations to the SASRec rows, with the SASRec binary cross-entropy loss replaced by the sampled-softmax loss in both.

priors.statement: The one structural change this repository publishes end to end is depth for per-head width at a fixed total attention width: HSTU → HSTU-large is blocks 2→8, heads 1→2 and dqk/dv 50→25 on ML-1M, i.e. num_heads × dqk stays equal to item_embedding_dim (50).
priors.evidence: configs/ml-1m/hstu-sampled-softmax-n128-final.gin: num_blocks 2, num_heads 1, dqk 50, dv 50. configs/ml-1m/hstu-sampled-softmax-n128-large-final.gin: num_blocks 8, num_heads 2, dqk 25, dv 25. Both keep item_embedding_dim 50 and every training hyperparameter identical. The same invariant holds on the other datasets: ML-20M 4 heads × 64 → 8 × 32 at item_embedding_dim 256; Amazon 4 × 16 → 8 × 8 at 64.

priors.statement: hr@10 and ndcg@10 are not independent: both are driven by the rank of the single held-out target, ndcg weighted by 1/log2(rank+1). A change can raise ndcg@10 while hr@10 is flat only by moving hits up the list, and can raise hr@10 while ndcg@10 falls only by adding hits at low positions — which is why ndcg@10 is the guardrail and not a second primary.
priors.evidence: eval.py computes `eval_ranks` from the target's position in the top-k ids, then hr@k = (rank <= k) and ndcg@k = where(rank <= k, 1/log2(rank+1), 0). Both are per-example tensors averaged by `_avg` over the eval loader.

priors.statement: An epoch's eval is truncated to `partial_eval_num_iters` batches unless the epoch is a full-eval epoch, and a truncated value is not comparable to a full one — it is measured on a different, shuffled subset of the eval loader.
priors.evidence: train.py breaks out of the eval loop after `partial_eval_num_iters` iterations when `full_eval_every_n` does not divide the epoch, logging 'Truncating epoch N eval to M iters to save cost..'; then it logs the epoch's numbers anyway. The ML-1M configs leave full_eval_every_n at its default 1 (never truncated); the Amazon config sets 5 (four epochs in five truncated) and partial_eval_num_iters 64.

hypothesis_classes.description: let the model represent more functions — more blocks, a wider embedding table, or both
hypothesis_classes.expected_effect: the only class with a published end-to-end gain (+0.0197 HR@10 for 2→8 blocks at fixed width); costs GPU hours roughly linearly with blocks

hypothesis_classes.description: change how attention is shaped at a fixed embedding width — heads against per-head width, keeping num_heads × dqk = item_embedding_dim as the published configs do
hypothesis_classes.expected_effect: small, easy to confound with capacity; the published large variants halve per-head width to double heads

hypothesis_classes.description: change what the model knows about position and time — the bucketed relative bias, the learnable positional embedding, or neither
hypothesis_classes.expected_effect: unknown from this repository (no ablation published); a negative result here is worth as much as a positive one

hypothesis_classes.description: change the pointwise nonlinearity or the output projection — silu against none, with or without the u·a concatenation
hypothesis_classes.expected_effect: unknown from this repository; a plausible cheap win or a plausible no-op, which is why it is one candidate and not a sweep

hypothesis_classes.description: constrain the fit — dropout on the positional embedding, dropout inside the HSTU linear and attention paths, weight decay
hypothesis_classes.expected_effect: neutral-to-negative on a dataset this small unless the candidate is overfitting; the published ML-1M rows use 0.2/0.2 and no weight decay

hypothesis_classes.description: change the space the retrieval happens in — l2-normalised user embedding or layer-norm, l2-normalised item embedding or not, a different softmax temperature
hypothesis_classes.expected_effect: may move the ranking without changing what the model learned; the guardrail (ndcg@10) is what tells those two apart

hypothesis_classes.description: change the loss the model is trained with — SampledSoftmaxLoss against BCELoss
hypothesis_classes.expected_effect: the README's own comparison changed the loss for its baselines, so this is a real structural axis, but a loss change also changes what 'converged' means: budget for it as the round's expensive candidate

forbidden_directions: Any change outside the adjustable surface: main.py, research/trainer/train.py, research/data/*, requirements.txt, or the other datasets' configs. An adjuster that can edit the evaluation cannot be compared with one that cannot.
Anything that moves the measurement instead of the model: eval_interval, full_eval_every_n, partial_eval_num_iters, eval_batch_size, save_ckpt_every_n.
Anything that changes the benchmark: dataset_name, max_sequence_length, num_negatives, sampling_strategy, or the split/sequence construction in research/data.
Optimizer retuning as a co-change (learning_rate, num_warmup_steps, local_batch_size). A structural gain measured against a baseline with a different learning rate belongs to neither.
Switching the family (main_module) — that redefines the baseline instead of improving it.
Numeric-precision switches (enable_tf32) or dependency upgrades: they move the number and cannot be attributed to structure.
A knob value outside `search_space`, or a combination the `constraints` above say will crash.
